stories.headline: 'No national security risk': Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as president, CEO
stories.title: 'No national security risk': Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as president, CEO
stories.summary: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and board director, less than two weeks after he resigned. The board voted unanimously after meetings with Huang and input from senior US government officials, saying his return poses no national security risk. Interim CEO Colette Kress continues as CFO. An independent probe into reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort will continue as Nvidia tightens compliance.

stories.headline: No Winter Session of Parliament? Skipped only four times in history
stories.title: No Winter Session of Parliament? Skipped only four times in history
stories.summary: Each previous instance coincided with extraordinary disruptions, from the Emergency and Lok Sabha dissolutions to Indira Gandhi’s assassination and the COVID-19 pandemic
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Winter Session of Parliament has been skipped only four times in India’s parliamentary history, and each instance was linked to exceptional circumstances, including the Emergency, the premature dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

With the Monsoon Session yet to be prorogued, setting a record for Parliament remaining unprorogued for more than 100 days, speculation has grown over the possibility of a short special session to consider the delimitation Bill.
The absence of any move to summon Parliament for its customary winter sitting has also fuelled discussion about whether the session could be skipped altogether.
The first time Parliament missed its winter session was during the 19-month Emergency.
The Lok Sabha met from July 21 to August 7, 1975, and then only from January 5 to February 6, 1976, without sitting during November or December, when the Winter Session is normally held.
The next instance came in 1979 after the premature dissolution of the Sixth Lok Sabha on August 22.
The newly elected House met only in January 1980, resulting in the Winter Session being skipped.
A similar situation arose in 1984 following the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on October 31.
General elections were called, and the Eighth Lok Sabha held its first sitting on January 15, 1985.
After a gap of 36 years, the Winter Session was skipped again in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Amid fears over the spread of the virus and stringent social-distancing norms, Parliament did not meet after the truncated Monsoon Session that ran from September 14 to 23.
In the 12 years of the Narendra Modi government, the timing of the Winter Session has varied considerably.

stories.headline: How India is rolling out the red carpet for the big, fat wedding
stories.title: How India is rolling out the red carpet for the big, fat wedding
stories.summary: Europe was a serious contender when Kinjal Shah was planning her wedding, scheduled for March 2027. Her fiancé’s immediate family lived in the US, and it made sense to bring the two sides together there for a function with 100 guests representing the bride and groom. Shah, though, was keen on a traditional Indian wedding, rooted in the country’s culture.“I wanted a maximal Indian wedding, with all the rituals, outfits and ceremonies. I wanted that authenticity, and I managed to convince my fiancé about it,” she tells Forbes India.Shah chose Udaipur because its palaces and heritage hotels offered the royal setting she had imagined. Also, its network of local vendors made the many moving parts of a wedding easier to organise. “You have several options for each requirement. If you need something, you can find multiple vendors instead of having to arrange everything from distant cities,” the wedding planner explains.Also Read: Why luxury's biggest bet on India might be its costliest mistake A San Francisco-based couple brought their closest friends and family to Fairmont Jaipur for their wedding. Photo by The Wedding FilesShah’s is not an isolated case. Indians are increasingly warming up to a location within the country for their big day. And the government is leaving no stone unturned to pursue wealthy Indians, be it locals or NRIs, to keep their wedding spending at home.It has launched initiatives like ‘Wed in India’ and ‘India says I do’ to ensure that NRIs and foreign couples consider the country as a wedding destination. In his ‘Mann Ki Baat’ broadcast in November 2023, Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged wealthy families to consider hosting weddings in India, which laid the foundation for ‘Wed in India’. The Ministry of Tourism had already launched its ‘India Says I Do’ campaign in August 2023, aimed at showcasing the country’s palaces, heritage monuments, beaches, mountains and temples to couples around the world. An Indian wedding taking place at Taj Gorbandh Palace in Jaisalmer in February. Photo by Raabta by Shrey BhagatBoost to economyWhen affluent Indian families take their weddings abroad, much of the money spent on hotels, venues, entertainment and hospitality leaves the economy with them. As destination weddings take place in India, guests spend at restaurants, on shopping and sightseeing. People who travel from overseas extend their stay and explore other locations, spreading the benefit. Devanshi Patel, founder of Shreem Events, points to a chain in Udaipur—a place with high underemployment—where a wedding creates work for florists, fabricators, technicians, folk dancers, musicians, photographers and make-up artists. “If this kind of money, which otherwise goes outside India, stays in India, it’s obviously going to bring the country into the top charts of the wedding industry,” she says.Amrit Arora, founder of The Wedding Files, a wedding photography service, explains that a wedding brings together a network of professionals. “During the pandemic, when weddings were disrupted, we saw how that disruption affected businesses across this ecosystem. The return of celebrations reinforced how many livelihoods depend on the wedding industry functioning well,” he says.States also acknowledge how destination weddings can power local ecosystems. “They undoubtedly create opportunities for local vendors and service providers, while encouraging guests to extend their stays and explore the destination,” says Kedar Naik, director of tourism, Goa.If keeping Indian weddings at home aims at retaining domestic expenditure, bringing foreign weddings to India is about attracting new spending from NRIs and couples who may otherwise choose places such as Thailand, the UAE or Europe.“About 25 percent of the world’s weddings take place in India. The ministry is developing a national wedding tourism digital database, issuing a standard format to obtain destination information covering event capacity, accommodation, facilities, etc,” says a senior official from the tourism ministry on condition of anonymity.Also Read: An ode to love: The big, fat Indian wedding is back with a bangWow for VowsIndia, the stakeholders believe, has the right ingredients for hosting intimate weddings. It’s just that there is a need for making a noise about it.Chetan Vohra, chairperson of FICCI’s Wed in India taskforce, and chairman and managing director of WeddingLine, a wedding planning company, says: “Wed in India is an obvious extension of Incredible India. We’ve done wildlife and medical tourism, and a whole lot more, but there was never a focus on weddings and the industry is massive.”His taskforce works with state governments to identify what is needed to support destination weddings [in India] and wedding tourism. “The idea is to give states the leverage to realise what they need to do to boost wedding tourism, bring everybody up to a certain level, and then unleash an aggressive international campaign saying that all of India is ready to host weddings,” Vohra tells Forbes India. “We have culture, tradition, monuments, temples, beaches, mountains, everything that the world can offer on one canvas.”Several states, especially the ones known as popular wedding destinations, are already taking the lead in this regard. Naik of the Goa government says the coastal state is contributing to India’s broader ambition by coordinating closely with the stakeholders.“Through destination marketing, participation on tourism platforms and engagement with industry stakeholders, we continue to showcase our strengths to wider audiences.By combining quality hospitality with cultural authenticity and local experiences, we can elevate our share,” he says.Desi vs ForeignOne of the biggest and most-talked-about functions that put India in the spotlight as a wedding destination was the Anant Ambani-Radhika Merchant marriage in 2024. The grandeur and scale of the months-long celebrations—from pre-wedding festivities in Jamnagar that included performances by celebrities like Rihanna and Katy Perry, to the final ceremonies in Mumbai—changed the way India’s wedding industry was perceived globally.Also Read: Raj Mantena: The low-profile tycoon behind the viral Udaipur wedding“Wherever we travelled internationally, the first thing anybody would talk about was the Ambani wedding,” says Madhulika Mathur, co-founder and director of WeddingSutra, a bridal media and wedding planning platform. “Some of the high-profile weddings in India are now being discussed among the movers and shakers around the world.”Global attention, though, does not automatically translate into foreign bookings, and the Ambani wedding is not a template every family can replicate. Other factors such as rising hotel costs and the geopolitical situation are also issues that compel people to reconsider hosting their wedding in the country.“India is not a viable destination as of now. It might be frightfully expensive. There has been a 25 to 30 percent increase in hotel prices, maybe more in some places. Our biggest challenge is to get everybody to understand that it has to be made a viable destination,” says Vohra.According to Anjali Tolani, vice president of celebrations at Tamarind Global, a wedding planning company, beyond the destination, expenses related to accommodation, food and beverage, décor and production, entertainment, transportation and guest logistics are also evaluated before making a final decision. “When these components are assessed together, a destination that initially appears more affordable may not necessarily offer better value. An alternative location may allow a family to achieve a more ambitious experience within the same budget,” she says.Foreign locations also have an edge when it comes to the ease of dealing with the government for allowances and permissions.“Permissions and sign-offs make it a little tedious to have a wedding in India,” says Kavneet Sethi, founder of The Wedding Galore, a Thailand-based company which plans Indian weddings. “In Thailand, it’s smooth sailing. You come to the property, see it, like it, sign a deal and that’s it,” she continues, adding that Thai tourism authorities offer incentives and do everything to attract Indian families for a wedding there.Agrees Patel of Shreem Events, who is also a part of the Wed in India campaign. “Internationally, they give you a blanket permission,” she says. “In India, there will be a music licence, alcohol licence, venue licence, police permission, gram panchayat licence, beach licence. It just doesn’t end.”The ease of execution must become as important as the destination’s appeal, according to Tolani. “The experience of planning and delivering a largescale celebration can still be considerably more complex than it needs to be.” So, to compete with Thailand, India needs to learn how the country makes it easier to have a wedding there. The official quoted earlier says the tourism ministry aims to establish simplified approval mechanisms and streamline, in particular, GST-related and music licensing-related issues, by December.‘I Do’ in IndiaDespite the bottlenecks and hurdles, high net-worth individuals (HNI) and ultra-high net-worth individuals (UHNI) are opting for India to host weddings. Planners call this a market shaped by several forces at once: The government’s message, new venue supply and the West Asia crisis.Monil Shah, founder and CEO of Kkings Events, talks about the impact of geopolitics. He says he knows of three weddings that were scheduled to be held in the Middle East but were shifted to India this year because the families and guests did not want to deal with uncertainty. Another couple who initially wanted to marry inAlUla in Saudi Arabia eventually chose Adiyogi in Tamil Nadu. “A strategy was built around it, and they were guided to push something in India instead,” he says.Patel has dealt with multiple instances of weddings being shifted from an overseas location to India. One of her clients changed the destination from Abu Dhabi to Rishikesh, while another wedding planned in Sri Lanka moved to the family’s hometown of Ahmedabad, turning a three-day celebration into a nine-day event. “Families want greater certainty and do not want to expose their guests to travel-related risks,” she says.According to Tolani, for NRIs, a wedding in India is much more than a celebration. “It is an opportunity to reconnect with their roots, bring extended families together and share their heritage with a wider circle of friends, including those who may be experiencing India for the first time.”For many affluent families, a luxury Indian wedding means celebrations over two to three days, sometimes even longer. The rituals are central, connecting the festivities to family, faith and regional culture.Mathur tells Forbes India that the emphasis on personalisation has made luxury Indian weddings more labour-intensive than ever. There are florists, fabricators, musicians, technicians and hospitality teams who collaborate with planners to create an experience.A 2025-26 report by WedMeGood, a digital wedding planning platform, puts the average Indian wedding budget at ₹39.5 lakh, up 8 percent from the previous year. The average budget for a destination wedding in India, in contrast, was ₹58 lakh. More than 60 percent of weddings that cost ₹1 crore or more were held away from home, while 89 percent of destination weddings took place within India.Before Covid, 400 to 600 guests were common in Indian weddings, but that number fell during the pandemic, at times due to government regulations on social gatherings; in 2025, weddings with 600 to 800 guests were again being hosted, with budgets averaging ₹15 crore to ₹20 crore among Kkings Events’ Shah’s clientele. “The Covid phase opened a new segment of intimate weddings, where the spend was big, around ₹5 crore, but only with 100 people,” he says. “The experience was much larger for them. Both segments—intimate and large—are now doing well.”The hotel industry is witness to the change on ground. Nivedan Kukreti, general manager, Taj Corbett Resort, says they have seen an increase in inquiries and bookings from NRIs over the last few years. “Many overseas families are rediscovering India as a wedding destination because it offers something incredibly unique. While costs have certainly risen across the hospitality industry, we have not seen a significant impact on the appetite for luxury weddings,” he says.The luxury market in India may be smaller by volume, but it is disproportionately large in footprint. WeddingSutra’s Annual Luxury and Destination Weddings Survey 2026 found that around 50 percent of UHNIs choose destination celebrations for at least a pre- or post-wedding event, compared with 12 percent of HNIs. And some venues are more favoured than the others.Melting Pot of cultureRajasthan remains the clearest expression of the luxury proposition. Udaipur, Jaipur, Jodhpur and Jaisalmer offer palace hotels, heritage, architecture and dramatic landscapes. “It’s not just the palaces,” Shah says. “The cultural heritage is visible throughout the city.”But the popularity has created a capacity problem. A survey by WeddingSutra, a digital media and wedding planning brand, found that several of Udaipur’s top palace properties are now largely accessible only to UHNIs in peak season, with Jaipur increasingly seen as a cheaper alternative outside the peak period. Shah of Kkings Events reveals that a hotel charged ₹30,000 for bed and breakfast one year and ₹65,000 the next. “A 100 percent increase in a year is unreal,” he says. “It is only because the volume of weddings has increased while the supply is low… that is inflating prices.”If Rajasthan offers heritage, Goa offers a vibe. “With its premium beachfront resorts, luxury hotels, heritage properties, diverse cuisine and established hospitality ecosystem, Goa offers a range of settings for celebrations,” says Naik.Demand is also calendar-bound in India, says Mathur, mainly between mid-January and early May, with February particularly busy.But India cannot depend on Rajasthan or Goa alone. Dehradun and Kerala remain popular, while Kochi, Mahabalipuram, Coorg, Alibaug and Karjat are gaining attention. The WeddingSutra survey also lists Bekal, Amritsar, Rishikesh, Mussoorie, Ramnagar, Agra and Sawai Madhopur among places seeing stronger demand, helped by better connectivity and new four- and five-star hotels.Also Read: Quiet luxury in India: Elites embrace global trend, redefining it on their own termsShah sees spiritual weddings as the next frontier, in places such as Ayodhya, Varanasi, Dwarka, Madurai, Rishikesh, Pushkar, Rameshwaram, Ujjain and Maheshwar. “The format is a small, intimate celebration with closest family members at a location related to spirituality, and somewhere nearby, a grand celebration with the larger audience,” he says.While Thailand offers a lesson in packaging a destination, Sethi concedes that weddings from India in the country have eased, partly because of the government’s call to host at home, but NRI weddings continue. She estimates a typical luxury budget for a 250-person, two-to-three-day wedding in Thailand at around ₹3 crore. Patel puts a lavish 200-person wedding in Udaipur at ₹5-10 crore, against ₹1-4 crore in Khao Lak, Phuket or Bali. Guests gather at a wedding reception at Umaid Bhawan Palace in Jodhpur, Rajasthan. Photo by Olivier Polet / Corbis via Getty ImagesBeyond the weddingAside from the direct wedding economy, a grand Indian wedding also impacts the peripheral industries. Intra-city travel is one such big opportunity. Aman Naagar, managing director of Avis India, which offers chauffeur-driven car services, says a wedding with 200 to 300 guests can require 30 to 50 vehicles. “Even a mid-sized wedding means well over 100 days of paid work for drivers,” he says. “That’s before you count the coordinators on the ground and the fleet owners who supply the vehicles.”During peak season, in Jaipur or Udaipur, several weddings can overlap. “Those are the weeks when local operators are fully booked, and many of them earn a big share of their annual business in those few months,” he adds.That said, there is still more work to be done in positioning India as one of the most coveted choices for weddings. Rising hotel prices, limited rooms, seasonal demand and uneven infrastructure persist, while Thailand and the UAE compete on predictable logistics and strong ecosystems. “The opportunity is immense, but continued investment in infrastructure will be critical,” Kukreti says.Vohra, though, is optimistic. “Given India’s history of hospitality, I think we are definitely on a path to becoming one of the top two or three wedding destinations in the world,” he says. “The number of jobs we give, the employment that goes out, the taxes we contribute with and the revenue we generate are tremendous. We need a lot more to happen, including the government giving us proper industry status.”Tolani says the government’s efforts are necessary; however, sustained success will depend on translating that intent into measurable improvements on ground. “India does not need to compete solely on grandeur or heritage. It needs to compete on a complete proposition. A globally competitive wedding destination combines an extraordinary setting with ease of access, regulatory clarity, service consistency and value,” she says.The government and stakeholders have rolled out the red carpet. It’s just a matter of time before the wedding bells start ringing louder in the country. “India has great infrastructure, great flexibility with weddings, great promotions and great tourism support to build on. If India decides to make that mark globally, it can do it,” says Patel.

“With its premium beachfront resorts, luxury hotels, heritage properties, diverse cuisine and established hospitality ecosystem, Goa offers a range of settings for celebrations,” says Naik.
Demand is also calendar-bound in India, says Mathur, mainly between mid-January and early May, with February particularly busy.
But India cannot depend on Rajasthan or Goa alone.
Dehradun and Kerala remain popular, while Kochi, Mahabalipuram, Coorg, Alibaug and Karjat are gaining attention.

The WeddingSutra survey also lists Bekal, Amritsar, Rishikesh, Mussoorie, Ramnagar, Agra and Sawai Madhopur among places seeing stronger demand, helped by better connectivity and new four- and five-star hotels.
Shah sees spiritual weddings as the next frontier, in places such as Ayodhya, Varanasi, Dwarka, Madurai, Rishikesh, Pushkar, Rameshwaram, Ujjain and Maheshwar.
“The format is a small, intimate celebration with closest family members at a location related to spirituality, and somewhere nearby, a grand celebration with the larger audience,” he says.

While Thailand offers a lesson in packaging a destination, Sethi concedes that weddings from India in the country have eased, partly because of the government’s call to host at home, but NRI weddings continue.
She estimates a typical luxury budget for a 250-person, two-to-three-day wedding in Thailand at around ₹3 crore.
Patel puts a lavish 200-person wedding in Udaipur at ₹5-10 crore, against ₹1-4 crore in Khao Lak, Phuket or Bali.
Guests gather at a wedding reception at Umaid Bhawan Palace in Jodhpur, Rajasthan.

Intra-city travel is one such big opportunity.
Aman Naagar, managing director of Avis India, which offers chauffeur-driven car services, says a wedding with 200 to 300 guests can require 30 to 50 vehicles.
“Even a mid-sized wedding means well over 100 days of paid work for drivers,” he says.
“That’s before you count the coordinators on the ground and the fleet owners who supply the vehicles.” During peak season, in Jaipur or Udaipur, several weddings can overlap.
“Those are the weeks when local operators are fully booked, and many of them earn a big share of their annual business in those few months,” he adds.
That said, there is still more work to be done in positioning India as one of the most coveted choices for weddings.
Rising hotel prices, limited rooms, seasonal demand and uneven infrastructure persist, while Thailand and the UAE compete on predictable logistics and strong ecosystems.
“The opportunity is immense, but continued investment in infrastructure will be critical,” Kukreti says.
Vohra, though, is optimistic.
“Given India’s history of hospitality, I think we are definitely on a path to becoming one of the top two or three wedding destinations in the world,” he says.
“The number of jobs we give, the employment that goes out, the taxes we contribute with and the revenue we generate are tremendous.

We need a lot more to happen, including the government giving us proper industry status.” Tolani says the government’s efforts are necessary; however, sustained success will depend on translating that intent into measurable improvements on ground.
“India does not need to compete solely on grandeur or heritage.
It needs to compete on a complete proposition.
A globally competitive wedding destination combines an extraordinary setting with ease of access, regulatory clarity, service consistency and value,” she says.
The government and stakeholders have rolled out the red carpet.
It’s just a matter of time before the wedding bells start ringing louder in the country.
“India has great infrastructure, great flexibility with weddings, great promotions and great tourism support to build on.
If India decides to make that mark globally, it can do it,” says Patel.

stories.title: Supreme Court flags ‘active connivance’ of civic authorities in ‘flagrant’
stories.summary: The court seeks suggestions from States and Union Territories on how to address such flagrant violations of building bye-laws
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Monday (November 23, 2026) observed that unauthorised constructions often flourished with the “active connivance” of civic authorities in the hope that State governments would eventually regularise such structures, particularly ahead of elections.
The court sought suggestions from States and Union Territories on how to address such flagrant violations of building bye-laws.
“The state of municipal inspection in our cities, for example, is in shambles, to say the least.
It is often undertaken after the building has risen and the violation has become a fait accompli.
Such inspections are, to say the least, a sham.

It is also an open secret that unauthorised construction often flourishes with the active connivance of municipal authorities, hoping that State governments would ultimately regularise the same, particularly before an impending election,” a Bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Sanjeev Sachdeva observed.
The Bench was hearing a case arising from Tamil Nadu concerning construction in violation of land-use norms and building bye-laws.
The proceedings had earlier been heard extensively by a Bench headed by Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah, which had expanded the ambit of the case to examine similar violations across the country.

It had sought details from civic bodies in several State capitals on action taken against illegal constructions, besides issuing contempt notices to officials for failing to comply with its directions.
The case was, however, recently reassigned to the Bench headed by Justice Nagarathna following an administrative decision by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant.

Another public interest litigation, which arose from a private university student’s grievance, was subsequently expanded into a nationwide judicial inquiry on the functioning of private universities, including concessions granted to them, was also transferred from Justice Amanullah’s Bench.

On Monday (November 23, 2026), the Bench headed by Justice Nagarathna pointed to the “practical difficulties” of monitoring building bye-law violations nationwide, noting that differing regulations across States and Union Territories made it impractical to issue omnibus directions.

stories.title: CJI-led Bench Of Supreme Court To Hear Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam Bail Pleas On Nov 25
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court is set to hear bail pleas of former JNU scholar Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in the 2020 Delhi riots larger conspiracy case after the Delhi High Court denied them bail recently.
A bench comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana will hear the appeals on Wednesday(November 25).

It may be recalled that on January 5, 2026, a bench comprising Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice NV Anjaria denied bail to Imam and Khalid, calling them "ideological drivers" of the larger conspiracy.
It, however, granted bail to five other accused persons, including Gulfisha Fatima, by distinguishing the roles played by them in the alleged conspiracy.

While denying bail, the Court imposed a one-year embargo on the grant of bail and stated that Imam and Khalid can approach the Court upon the completion of protected witnesses' examination or upon expiry of 1 year from passing the order, "whichever is earlier".
The petitioners have filed the present appeal, submitting that the Supreme Court's one-year embargo imposed on the grant of bail is to expire soon.
They also said that the other condition imposed by the Court for examination of protected witnesses by the prosecution cannot possibly be completed by January 5, 2027.
Therefore, in light of prolonged incarceration, they be granted bail, the pleas urged.

reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has appointed former judge Justice Sanjay Karol as chairperson of a reconstituted Special Committee to resolve competing claims over plots in the Okhla Enclave project in Faridabad, Haryana.

A bench of Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Sandeep Mehta passed the order in a batch of applications arising from the long-pending dispute concerning the residential project in Faridabad, while also granting claimants who failed to submit their documents earlier a final three-week opportunity to do so.

Justice Karol replaces former Supreme Court judge Justice Vikramajit Sen, who resigned as Committee chairperson after concerns arose over local Town and Country Planning Department (DTCP) officials sanctioning building plans for 480 claimants whose title documents had not been verified.

Describing the dispute as one involving several competing claims and administrative irregularities, the Court observed that “the factual matrix of the present dispute has been complicated beyond imagination by a multiplicity of judicial and administrative proceedings spanning nearly four decades, overlapping categories of claimants, and glaring discrepancies in the numerical data emerging across various records.”
The project, spread over approximately 235 acres, has been embroiled in litigation over alleged unauthorised and duplicate allotments, incomplete development work and competing claims to plots.
The Court noted that 2,036 claims had been received for Phase II scrutiny, including 1,637 supported by registered sale deeds, 102 by powers of attorney and 297 by other documents.
Preliminary checks had revealed duplicate sale deeds relating to identical plots.
The Court also highlighted the acute shortage of available land.
Although 1,011 allottees had already been found eligible in Phase.
I, only around 150 vacant plots were reportedly available against 866 verified No Profit No Loss (NPNL) allottees.
Similarly, 49 verified General Category allottees were competing for just one vacant plot.
The Court noted that “the physical handing of possession is stalled owing to severe physical inventory deficit.”

stories.headline: West Bengal Govt Approaches Supreme Court Against HC Order Deferring Kolkata Municipal Elections
stories.title: West Bengal Govt Approaches Supreme Court Against HC Order Deferring Kolkata Municipal Elections
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The West Bengal Government has approached the Supreme Court challenging a Calcutta High Court order deferring the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) elections until a pending challenge to the delimitation of municipal wards is decided.
A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana heard the matter on Friday.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta appeared for the State Government.
After hearing the SG for some time, the bench adjourned the hearing till another day.

The challenge before the Supreme Court arises from a November 6 order passed by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court, which restrained the West Bengal State Election Commission from proceeding with the KMC elections until the pending challenge to the ward delimitation exercise is finally decided by a single judge.
The dispute concerns the West Bengal Government's decision to increase the number of wards in the Kolkata Municipal Corporation from 144 to 209 ahead of the municipal elections.
The State Government issued a delimitation notification on September 11, 2026, redrawing the boundaries of the municipal wards.
The exercise was challenged before the Calcutta High Court on the ground that it was undertaken without a valid recommendation from the elected Municipal Corporation.

The petitioners questioned the authority of Smita Pandey, who had been appointed Administrator of the KMC after the elected Corporation ceased to function, to make the recommendation for delimitation.
They argued that an Administrator could not substitute the elected Municipal Corporation for the purpose of making such a recommendation.
The petitioners also alleged that the redrawing of ward boundaries amounted to gerrymandering intended to give an electoral advantage to a particular political party.
A single judge of the High Court had earlier declined to stay the delimitation exercise.

stories.headline: Gold snaps 10-day losing run, rises Rs 1,500 to Rs 1.26 lakh/10gm
stories.title: Gold snaps 10-day losing run, rises Rs 1,500 to Rs 1.26 lakh/10gm
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 23: Gold prices snapped a 10-session losing streak, climbing Rs 1,500 to Rs 1.26 lakh per 10 grams in the national capital on Monday on local demand and strong global trends. The yellow metal of 99.9 per cent purity appreciated by Rs 1,500 to Rs 1,26,800 per 10 grams (inclusive of all taxes) from Saturday's close of Rs 1,25,300 per 10 grams, according to local traders. Silver also rebounded by Rs 2,000 to Rs 1.57 lakh per kg from Rs 1.55 lakh per kg in the preceding session. "Gold prices moved higher on Monday, tracking gains in global markets and expectations of improved jewellery demand amid the ongoing wedding season," said Saumil Gandhi, Senior Analyst of Commodities at HDFC Securities. The recent correction has brought prices to more attractive levels for consumers, while seasonal buying interest is expected to strengthen as the wedding season advances, Gandhi said. A similar improvement in physical demand was reported in India and China last week, reflecting renewed consumer interest after the price decline, he added. According to Akshat Siddhant, Lead Quant Analyst at investment platform Mudrex, lower domestic prices have also drawn bargain hunters back to physical gold. A marginal weakening of the rupee also supported prices. In international markets, spot gold gained USD 84.27, or 2.38 per cent, to USD 3,622.38 per ounce, while silver appreciated by 3.3 per cent to USD 42.59. "Gold has rebounded by over 2 per cent to near USD 3,630 per ounce after a 9 per cent weekly fall to a 14-month low, as traders pared December Fed rate hike bets after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned against overtightening," said Siddhant. Jateen Trivedi, VP Research Analyst - Commodity and Currency, LKP Securities, said market participants would focus on key US economic releases, including inflation and GDP data, which could provide fresh cues on inflation, economic growth and the Federal Reserve's future interest-rate trajectory. Looking ahead, volatility in bullion is likely to remain elevated amid movement in dollar and global economic developments, he added.

stories.title: India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
stories.summary: As Nepal rebuilds after deadly floods, its prime minister sets contentious issues aside to secure Indian funding, port access and a new train service.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours.
His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.
The contrast between the two leaders was striking.
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white.
Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations.
They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing.
